open-question.question: What is the new list flag called, and what line shape does it print for each block — how are the id and the folded question text separated on one line so that an id containing spaces, punctuation, or the separator itself stays unambiguous to a reader?
open-question.recommendation: The tool's fold collapses every whitespace run to one space on every write, so neither an id nor a question can hold a tab and the separator is unambiguous by construction while the one-line, bare, un-escaped read contract stays intact; the em dash can occur in free-text ids, quoting adds a read-side escaping rule, and the two-line record drops the one-line shape asked for.
open-question.alternative: Add a --with-question flag to list that prints each block on one line in document order: the id, a single tab, then the question's text, both un-escaped. Neither value can ever contain a tab, because every write folds each text and attribute value with a whitespace split, which turns every tab into one space. Nothing can make it ambiguous, because the separator cannot occur in either value. An id with spaces, ampersands, angle brackets, quotes, an em dash, or a colon stays exact. The read contract of bare, un-escaped values, one line per block, still holds, now with two tab-separated fields. The flag name also matches the existing --without-alternatives and --without-recommendation pattern. A tab looks like ordinary whitespace in a terminal or in a model's view of tool output. A reader cannot see where an id with spaces ends unless it knows the separator is a tab, so the contract has to state the separator in the docstring, the argparse help, and the output contract. Tests have to check for a literal tab rather than a visible mark.

Add a --with-question flag that prints each block on one line as the id, then space, em dash, space, then the question's text. This is the same separator lift already uses between an option and its rationale. It is easy to read, and it reuses a separator that the tool contract and the answer procedures already know from lift, so it adds no new output idiom. Nothing stops an id or a question from containing space, em dash, space itself, because Short Titles are free text. For an id like that, the split point is ambiguous by construction. The only protection is splitting at the first occurrence, which is correct only while the id itself holds no em dash. The question explicitly asks for protection against exactly this case.

Add a --with-question flag that prints each block as two lines: the bare id flush left, then the question's text on the next line indented by two spaces. Any line starting at column 0 is an id, and any indented line is that id's question. It is unambiguous both visually and by construction: folding trims the ends of every value, so no id starts with whitespace, and no id or question contains a line break. The id reads exactly as the list output shows it, with no separator character to explain. It drops the one-line-per-block shape the question asks for and changes the read contract from one value per line to a fixed two-line record per block. Readers and tests have to handle pairs of lines, and the output is twice as long as the other options.

Add a --with-question flag that prints each block on one line as the id wrapped in double quotes, then a space, then the question's text. Any double quote inside the id is escaped with a backslash, so the id ends at the first unescaped closing quote. The id's boundary is visible and unambiguous whatever characters the id contains, including spaces, dashes, colons, and tabs. A human or model reader can see where the id stops without knowing about an invisible separator. It breaks the tool's rule that reads print bare, un-escaped values. It adds a new escaping rule to a read output, and consumers would have to reverse that rule before passing the id to locate or any other subcommand. That is the kind of escaping detail the runtime prose is not supposed to restate.

open-question.question: Does the new question-text flag combine with the existing --without-alternatives and --without-recommendation filters (printing the filtered blocks with their text), or is it refused alongside them so the flag stays a single-purpose whole-set listing?
open-question.recommendation: The flag is a line-shape switch and the filters are block selectors, so composing keeps each list option doing one independent job with no new refusal path in the error contract, and the cost is two crossed tests rather than a hand-written exclusion check that a later inline consumer would have to undo.
open-question.alternative: The question-text flag changes only the line shape of `list`. The `--without-alternatives` and `--without-recommendation` filters decide which blocks print exactly as they do now, alone or together, so `list --without-alternatives` with the new flag prints each bare block's id beside its folded question text. It keeps `list` one subcommand in which each option does one independent job. `cmd_list` changes in one spot (what it prints, not which blocks), no new refusal path is added to the error contract, and the three places the contract is stated only need the flag described as a shape switch. An inline runner that later wants the filtered set with its text can have it without another tool change. The only consumer the milestone's goal names, the dispatched agent's sibling scope, wants the whole unfiltered set. That makes the combined forms a surface with no current consumer that still needs its own tests in `tests/test_list.py`, both filters crossed with the flag, to stay covered.

The question-text flag is only for listing the whole set. Passing it with either `--without-alternatives` or `--without-recommendation` is refused as a usage error that exits non-zero and prints nothing, while the two filters stay freely combinable with each other. The flag's contract stays as narrow as its one purpose: every block's id and question text, for sibling scope. A caller can't ask for a filtered text listing that nobody designed or needs, so the flag can't gradually become a second way to gather filtered sets. It adds a refusal the tool doesn't have today. The rule is that the flag excludes both filters while the filters still combine with each other. A single argparse mutually exclusive group can't express that, so it needs a hand-written check in `cmd_list` that follows the error contract. It also needs refusal tests and a note in the docstring, the help text, and the error contract. If an inline runner later needs filtered text, the refusal has to be lifted in a further tool change.

open-question.question: The shared alternatives procedure's grounding step tells its reader to read open_questions.xml whole with the file-reading tool, and it is followed by both the dispatched agent (which must not) and the inline discuss-open-question skill (which may): does the shared step keep a runner-neutral wording that names the sibling scope without prescribing how it is obtained, leaving each consumer to state its own source, or does it carry both instructions?
open-question.recommendation: The shared analytical halves stay execution-neutral and name no runner class, exactly as the commit mechanics were kept out of them, so the step keeps only the rule that siblings bound the question and are never presumed settled while each consumer states its own source in its own step; the split wording would mirror agent-file mechanics in a third place, and the uniform list print contradicts discuss-open-question's reuse of its whole read.
open-question.alternative: Rewrite the sibling paragraph in step 1 of `core/shared/alternatives-procedure.md` so it keeps only the analytical rule and drops the instruction on how siblings are read. The rule is that sibling questions mark where this question ends, supply scope and nothing more, and are never presumed settled. Each consumer names its own source in its own step: `discuss-open-question` already does this with its step-2 whole read, and the agent's step 1 would name `locate` plus the new list flag. The shared file stays purely analytical and names no runner class and no reading mechanism. That matches how the file already hands off to consumers ("reuse that reading" of the caller's grounding). Neither consumer has to follow an instruction meant for the other, and a later change to how the agent gets sibling scope leaves the shared file untouched. Read alone, the procedure no longer says where sibling scope comes from, so each consumer must state its source or the rule has nothing to apply to. The file's "every locate, list, or lift is a tool call" sentence also loses its natural anchor: it must move into each consumer or stay as a detached general sentence.

Keep a source instruction in the shared step and split it by runner. A runner working inline in the conversation reads `open_questions.xml` whole with the file-reading tool. A dispatched runner gets its own block through `locate` and sibling scope through the new list flag, and never reads the file whole. Whoever opens the one shared file sees both allowed ways to get sibling scope next to the rule they serve. The dispatched-agent restriction is also stated where the enumeration grounding happens, not only in the agent file and in `CLAUDE.md`. The shared procedure would have to know about dispatch and name runner classes. It would also repeat, in a third place, mechanics that the agent file and the new `CLAUDE.md` invariant already own, and those copies could drift apart. It would name the new list flag, so its wording depends on how the "Question-text list line shape" sibling question settles. Each consumer also has to read past a branch that is not addressed to it.

Have the shared step give every consumer the same narrow source: sibling scope is the new list flag's id-and-question print, with no whole read. This works because enumeration forms no preference and never presumes a sibling settled, so it needs only each sibling's question text, not its embedded children. There is one instruction with no branching, fitted to what enumeration actually needs. Every consumer then grounds its option set on exactly the same sibling scope, so an inline enumeration and a dispatched one work from the same input. `discuss-open-question` already reads `open_questions.xml` whole in its step 2, because its pick half needs the siblings' embedded alternatives, and step 3 tells it to reuse that reading. A mandatory list call would add a redundant tool call or contradict that reuse. The shared file would also name the new flag, so it depends on how the "Question-text list line shape" sibling question settles. Whether sibling scope should ever include embedded alternatives turns on how the "Sibling locate allowance" sibling question settles.

open-question.question: With sibling scope supplied as one id-and-question line per block, may the dispatched agent still run locate on a sibling block (to see alternatives an earlier pass embedded on it) when it judges that bears on the boundary between two questions, or is its reading of the question document limited to its own block and the list print?
open-question.recommendation: Two fixed tool calls give every run the same context size and make the reading limit checkable, keep a sibling's recommendation and depends-on picks out of the agent's view so siblings stay scope only and never assumed settled, and hold in a parallel sweep where a located sibling could appear bare or annotated by timing; the judgment form varies per run, and the alternatives-only form needs a tool option no decision has added.
open-question.alternative: The dispatched agent reads the question document only through two tool calls: one `locate` of its own Short Title, and one run of the new question-text `list` flag for sibling scope. It never runs `locate` on a sibling. The agent file states this limit once, as its only source of sibling scope. This fits the Goal's rule that the agent fetches its sibling scope with the new list flag. The agent's context stays exactly the size the milestone is trying to reach. It also keeps the existing rule that siblings supply scope and nothing more: the agent never sees a sibling's `<recommendation>` or `<depends-on>` pick, so it cannot start treating that pick as settled. The behaviour is the same on every run, whether or not an earlier pass annotated a sibling. Sometimes a boundary can't be read from question text alone, for example when two questions are worded so they overlap and only a sibling's embedded options show where it actually ends. In that case the agent may list an option that belongs to the sibling, or leave out a real one. That weakens the set, and the set has to be complete now because it outlasts later decisions. How often this happens depends on how unambiguous the list print's id-and-question line turns out to be.

The agent may `locate` any sibling block whenever it judges that the sibling's embedded content bears on the boundary between the two questions. Everything the agent reads stays read-only and is used for reasoning only. Its default source of sibling scope is still the list print. The agent gets the most accurate view of the boundary when it needs one. A sibling already annotated by an earlier alternatives pass (for example, before a review pass added this question) shows exactly which options it covers, so they aren't duplicated here. The cost falls only on the runs that need it, since in a single sweep most siblings are still bare and a `locate` would add nothing. The limit is left to prose judgment, so how much of the question document an agent reads varies from run to run and can't be checked mechanically. A located sibling also prints any `<recommendation>` and `<depends-on>` it carries, which invites exactly the assumption about how a sibling settles that the enumeration is told never to make. In a parallel sweep, a sibling another agent is embedding at that moment may appear bare or annotated depending on timing, so the same agent could produce different results on different runs.

The agent may `locate` a sibling only if that sibling already carries alternatives, meaning the `--without-alternatives` list doesn't print it. It reads only that sibling's `<alternative>` elements as scope and explicitly ignores any recommendation or dependency elements on the block. The only thing a sibling locate can usefully add is embedded options that mark where the sibling ends, and this rule allows just that. The agent never reads a sibling's pick, so the rule that siblings are never assumed settled holds. Locates on bare siblings, which would only repeat the list print, are ruled out. The rule is more complicated. It needs an extra `list --without-alternatives` call, or a check that this depends on, and two conditions stated in the agent's prose. Ignoring the pick elements is still prose discipline: they are printed into the agent's context anyway, and nothing mechanical stops them from influencing it. The tool can't print alternatives alone, so this would need a new tool option, and the milestone has recorded no decision to add one.

open-question.question: When the CLAUDE.md whole-file allowance is reworded to name the inline runners, does it enumerate the skills by name (a list that must be maintained as skills change) or describe them as a class (for example, user-invoked skills running inline in the conversation) that any future inline runner falls under without an edit?
open-question.recommendation: The other layer-scoped invariants already speak of classes such as every file-changing user-invoked skill, and a class sits cleanly opposite the new dispatched-agent invariant so a future inline runner falls on the right side without an edit, whereas a name list or an example list goes silently stale with no build step or test reading CLAUDE.md, and the exclusion form hands the allowance to any consumer that is not an agent by default.
open-question.alternative: The allowance describes its holders as a class without naming any skill. For example, it covers a user-invoked skill running inline in the conversation, and a shared procedure followed by one, when it needs the whole set to reason over. Any present or future inline runner falls under it without an edit. It needs no upkeep and matches how CLAUDE.md already words its other layer-scoped invariants, such as "every file-changing user-invoked skill commits exactly its own paths". It also lines up with the dispatched-agent invariant it now sits beside, one class allowed and the other constrained, so the pair splits cleanly along the inline/isolated line and a new skill falls on one side by construction. It is less concrete. A reader can no longer see which runners actually use the allowance, and a shared procedure with both kinds of consumer, like alternatives-procedure.md, sits on the line and needs the class wording to handle it explicitly. The drawback also depends on how the question on the shared procedure's sibling-scope wording settles.

The reworded allowance lists the six inline runners that state the whole read today by name (review-milestone-requirements, recommend-all-open-questions, answer-all-open-questions-with-recommendation, discuss-open-question, ask-in-milestone-context, modify-milestone-goal). It also names the shared procedures they follow, alternatives-procedure.md for discuss-open-question and recommend-procedure.md, which are covered through their inline consumers. It is exact and can be checked. A maintainer can grep each named SKILL.md for its whole-read sentence and confirm the invariant matches the runtime one-to-one. Nothing is left to judgment about whether a borderline consumer qualifies, and CLAUDE.md already keeps hand-maintained enumerations of this kind, such as the skill pipeline list. The list has to be kept up to date by hand, and nothing enforces it. No build step or test reads CLAUDE.md, so a skill that is added, renamed, or retired, or one that gains or drops the whole read, makes the list silently wrong. A future inline runner that relies on the allowance would seem to break the invariant until someone edits the list.

The allowance is stated as a class rule, as in the class option, followed by a parenthetical naming today's inline runners as examples ("currently …"). The class decides who holds the allowance, and the names are there only to help a reader find them. It keeps both strengths. The class wording means a new inline runner never breaks the invariant, and the named examples let a maintainer find the runtime sites that state the allowance without searching the tree. The example list still goes out of date with nothing to catch it. It is harmless to the rule's meaning, but it misleads anyone who reads it as complete. It also adds exactly the kind of mirrored detail the "rationale only in CLAUDE.md" principle tries to keep out of the invariants.

The allowance stays unscoped but gains an exception clause. Any consumer except a dispatched agent may read the file directly for reasoning only. The inline runners are named implicitly as everything outside the new dispatched-agent invariant's scope. It is the smallest wording change. It adds one clause that points at the new dispatched-agent invariant instead of defining a second class. The two invariants cannot drift apart because one is defined as the other's complement, so no consumer falls in neither category. It does not literally name the inline runners, as the milestone goal's wording ("reworded to name the inline runners") asks. Any new kind of consumer that is neither an inline skill nor a dispatched agent, such as a headless chain step or a script, gets the whole-read allowance by default and never has to justify it.

open-question.question: The new dispatched-agent invariant covers both dispatched agents: does it constrain only what a dispatch prompt carries (what the orchestrator holds and the agent cannot fetch), or also forbid a dispatched agent any whole read of a tool-owned document, and if the latter, how does it leave the complete-task agent's whole read of TASKS_TODO.md (a file no tool owns) untouched?
open-question.recommendation: The ban belongs next to the allowance it narrows, inside the invariant that already governs the question document, where its scope to that one document is fixed by where it sits, so the dispatched-agent invariant stays a prompt-content rule true of both agents without qualification and complete-task's whole read of TASKS_TODO.md is never in reach; a tool-owned clause is empty for complete-task today and must dodge the test fixtures, and the narrowest-slice rule shifts meaning whenever a tool gains a subcommand.
open-question.alternative: The dispatched-agent invariant covers only what a prompt carries. The reading rule instead goes into the sole-writer invariant, right beside the reworded whole-file allowance: inline runners may read the question document whole, and dispatched agents reach it only through the tool. That makes one boundary sentence scoped to the tool's own document, so it never reaches `TASKS_TODO.md`. The ban sits next to the allowance it narrows and inside the invariant that already governs `open_questions.xml`. Its scope to that one document is therefore clear from where it sits. The complete-task agent is never mentioned and cannot be caught by it, and the new dispatched-agent invariant stays true of both agents without qualification. The rules on what a dispatched agent receives and what it may read end up in two different invariants (three, counting the return contracts). An editor changing an agent has to find and reconcile all of them. How cleanly the ban fits depends on how the allowance itself is worded, which is decided separately.

The new invariant covers only what a dispatch prompt carries: the orchestrator passes what it already holds and the agent cannot fetch itself. It says nothing about what an agent reads. The alternatives agent's ban on reading `open_questions.xml` whole lives only in that agent's own file, and in CLAUDE.md it follows from the reworded whole-file allowance, which names only the inline runners and so leaves dispatched agents out. The rule holds for both dispatched agents as written, and nothing changes for complete-task. Its prompt already carries only the task's `##` heading, and its whole reads of `TASKS_TODO.md`, `requirements.md`, and the pointer are never touched. There is no carve-out to write, and the invariant matches the Goal's first sentence exactly. The reading half of the milestone has no stated reason anywhere. Dispatched agents are excluded only because the reworded allowance leaves them off its list, which an editor can easily miss. So a later edit can bring back the alternatives agent's whole read (or add a new agent that does one), and no invariant visibly forbids it.

The invariant has two clauses. One limits what a dispatch prompt carries. The other says a dispatched agent reaches a tool-owned document (the milestone's question document) only through the tool, never by reading it whole. The second clause is keyed on the document's owner, so files no tool writes, such as `TASKS_TODO.md`, `TASKS_DONE.md`, `requirements.md`, and `milestones/README.md`, are outside it by construction, with no named exception. Both halves of the milestone get their reason recorded in one agent-scoped place. The complete-task agent needs no carve-out: its `TASKS_TODO.md` read is outside the clause because no tool owns that file, and the clause would still apply if a tool later took ownership of some other file. For complete-task the reading clause is empty today, since the completion procedure never opens the question document. So the claim that the invariant covers both agents is partly nominal. The clause also has to name the milestone's question document, not the filename `open_questions.xml`. Otherwise a completion task in this repo that edits `tests/fixtures/*/open_questions.xml` would read as a violation.

The invariant covers the prompt and adds a general reading rule: a dispatched agent fetches the narrowest slice a tool offers and reads whole only what no tool can slice. `TASKS_TODO.md` and `requirements.md` are left alone because no tool slices them. The question document is covered because `locate` and the new list flag slice it. It states the reason behind the whole milestone, keeping the agent's context small, as one general rule. It also extends to future tools without an edit: if a task-list tool later offers a per-task slice, the complete-task agent comes under the rule automatically. What the rule allows changes silently whenever a tool gains or loses a subcommand. So it cannot be checked against the text alone, and a new tool feature could quietly make an existing whole read in complete-task or the completion procedure a violation. It also pushes a reader to ask whether `requirements.md` should be sliced too, which the Goal explicitly keeps as a whole read.
